newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Blacklisted Colombia set to rent drug satellite.
newsitem.headline: Blacklisted Colombia set to rent drug satellite.

text.p: Colombia wants to rent its own spy-in-the sky satellite to chart "independently" the spread of illicit drug crops after a disagreement over the results of U.S. aerial imaging, a top counternarcotics agent said on Sunday.

Col. Leonardo Gallego said talks were under way to contract the services of a Canadian satellite after U.S. experts said images from their satellites showed Colombia's sprawling coca leaf and opium poppy plantations were expanding.

U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Robert Gelbard estimated clandestine drug crop cultivation increased by more than 30 percent last year -- one of the key factors behind Washington's decision on last Friday to "decertify" Colombia as an ally in the drug war for the second consecutive year.

Colombia says the claimed increase is exagerrated and points to its record of fumigating more than 62,400 acres (26,000 hectares) of coca leaf and opium poppy as evidence that it made massive strides on the road to winning the drug war.
"We're looking into the possibility of contracting a Canadian satellite with great interest in an effort to technify the fight against narco-trafficking," Gallego told the Radionet radio network.

"We hope the project comes off so that we have our own technology to carry out monitoring and an independent, objective evaluation (of the spread of drug crops). This is the second time we have major differences about this with the United States," he added.
The United States calculated the acreage of coca leaf -- the raw material for cocaine production -- increased from 122,400 acres (51,000 hectares) to 160,800 (67,000 hectares) in Colombia in 1996.
Gallego said it was unfair for the United States to criticise the expansion of drug plantations in areas which had not yet been targeted by the ambitious U.S. crop eradication programme.

Meanwhile, in a strike that Colombia is bound to use as evidence of its commitment to fighting drug trafficking with or without U.S. certification, the National Police said on Sunday it had destroyed a clandestine laboratory capable of producing six tonnes of cocaine a week in eastern Meta province. More than three tonnes of processed cocaine was seized in the operation, a police statement said.

The decision to decertify Colombia once again -- reducing it to the status of a virtual pariah nation alongside Burma, Afghanistan, Nigeria and Syria -- drew fierce reaction in Colombia. President Ernesto Samper and Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia have threatened a shake-up of all bilateral cooperation agreements with the United States.

And the country's three main labour federations have called an anti-American demonstration at the gates of the U.S. embassy in Bogota on Wednesday to protest what they say is "U.S. encroachment on national sovereignty."
